title: ADHD is not a self-control deficit, but a different way the nervous system processes the world
dek: Mainstream frameworks treat ADHD as an executive function deficit correctable through self-control; this counselor argues the root is inborn differences in attention regulation and sensory processing, traits that once were survival advantages for humans.
why: Directly challenges the most authoritative medical framework in ADHD discourse with specific counterexamples and evidence, rather than vague contrarianism.
who: Parents newly diagnosed with ADHD themselves or whose children are, those trapped by the "not enough self-control" narrative, and counselors seeking an alternative support framework.

points.h: Attention regulation, not executive function, is the root problem
points.body: The mainstream account traces ADHD to executive-function deficits, but B. Lourenco asks: why would executive function fail? She locates it instead in attention-regulation differences—not deficits but different regulation. The mechanism is sensory variation: the world is noisier, more intense, harder to screen out for ADHD brains. One theory she cites: ADHD may stem from early hunter-gatherer neurology, hence an interest-based nervous system—not a switch to do what you should, but constant alertness to what is that? because it could mean food or survival.

points.h: The lifespan gap is real, but the explanation is oversimplified
points.body: B. Lourenco acknowledges the data—ADHD people do have worse health outcomes and shorter lifespans—but rejects the pure impulse-control story. By that logic, living longer just means controlling yourself better, which doesn't hold. She points out that the medical model omits the comorbidities common in ADHD: mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, fibromyalgia. Those diseases themselves shorten life. If doctors fixate on impulse control, a patient with these comorbidities gets told to manage themselves, not screened for other conditions.

points.h: ADHD requires structure and design, not control as the answer
points.body: Against objections like "rules help everyone" (traffic laws), B. Lourenco draws a line between structure and control. ADHD does need structure and constraint—free-form chaos won't work for this nervous system. But treating control as the only answer is broken: it puts all burden on the ADHD person or parent, not the environment. It reinforces "if you wanted to, you could," which isn't true. There is an impulse-control piece, she allows, but the answer isn't more control. It's finding structures people actually adopt and stick with.

points.h: One household, two divergent medication histories
points.body: B. Lourenco has a child who was diagnosed and medicated for ADHD from childhood; she herself wasn't identified until adulthood. This split explains why she and the other parent clash on drugs. She tells listeners with similar childhood-medication histories: the problem wasn't just "too many kids on meds"—it was how much each kid took and that no one heard their voice. Those two wrongs—overdosing and silencing—can be separated; her child's path doesn't have to repeat them.

points.h: Whether children should have a right to refuse medication: they clash
points.body: The episode mentions ADHD authority Barkley's stance: prefrontal development is incomplete, so kids lack the capacity to decide; medication is 100 percent a parent call, kids' input irrelevant. B. Lourenco calls this infantilizing, a denial of the child's autonomy as a whole person. She allows that medication works fast and gets picked first for that reason—environmental change takes upkeep—but speed alone shouldn't make it eternal or primary. Drugs can be a starting point, not the only or forever top option.

points.h: One needs quiet, one craves noise: neither is wrong
points.body: When a parent desires calm but the child is wired for novelty and stimulation, B. Lourenco's first step: name it. Sensory need isn't chosen; it just is. This doesn't make anyone bad. But within the parent-child bond, the power is asymmetric. Parents bring more self-regulation skills and carry more load—a ratio that shifts with age. A four- to six-year-old can already understand "Mom needs quiet for a few minutes." B. Lourenco tells her kids she's taking a break and will be back—this normalizes her need and teaches them "Mom is a separate person from me."

points.h: Stop blaming yourself first; then find people who can hold you
points.body: Asked what to say to newly diagnosed or questioning parents, B. Lourenco offers two things. First: stop shaming and blaming yourself. Put ADHD on the human timeline—it's not a fundamental error. Diversity itself is why the human species endured. Second: build a real, shame-free, non-judgmental network. Call someone trusted and say "I'm about to break, give me ten minutes"; have them supervise the kid even by phone, or video-link a distant friend to watch for a while. Needing help doesn't mean you're broken; it means you're human.

points.h: Should society change for 5 percent of people
points.body: Jen closes with a memory: Barkley was asked, "Do we really reshape the whole society for 5 percent of the population?" His answer was a cold, scornful "No." Jen's is the opposite: yes—because designs that serve a marginalized group usually make life smoother for everyone. A routine that helps an ADHD kid get out the door on time usually helps the whole family's morning flow.
